_note: Spectrum position: 0 = instinct / infra-red (dense, warm, terrestrial) ... 1 = spirit / ultra-violet (clear, cool, fine); Jung, CW8 par. 414-420. `definitionPick` selects verbatim records from the vault's data/mentions.jsonl (vol + para + quote prefix) - the quote is never typed here. `body` is site prose and does not claim to be Jung's words.

self.name: The Self
self.oneLine: Totality of the psyche: the centre and circumference of conscious and unconscious.

definitionPick.starts: Psychologically the self is a union

body: The Self is where the map folds back on itself: the whole of the psyche, conscious and unconscious together, and the centre toward which a life is drawn. It is never met directly. It shows itself through images of wholeness, above all the circle and the quaternity.
On this globe the Self is the quiet field behind every other presence, reached through images as far apart as Upanishadic light and the alchemical stone.

shadow.name: Shadow
shadow.oneLine: The hidden, rejected side of the personality; everything we will not see in ourselves.

definitionPick.starts: The first of these is the SHADOW

body: The Shadow gathers what a person or a culture pushes out of sight: the guilty, the primitive, the unlived. It is met first because it is nearest, and it tends to arrive as an enemy, a double, a dark beast or a stranger on the stair.
Its images are dense and low in the spectrum: dragons, apes, the blackened sun, the devil as the other half of the sacred.

anima.name: Anima
anima.oneLine: The inner feminine in a man: life itself, personified as soul, muse and guide.
body: The Anima is the figure through which a man's unconscious turns toward him: siren and sophia, nymph and guide. She is watery, shifting and bipolar, and she draws the soul toward images rather than arguments.
She appears wherever a threshold is crossed by water, by song, by an unknown woman.

animus.name: Animus
animus.oneLine: The inner masculine in a woman: spirit, word and conviction.

definitionPick.starts: I have called the projection-making factor

body: The Animus is the masculine counterpart within a woman's psyche. It speaks as opinion and as spirit; at its best it is a bridge to the creative mind rather than a chorus of verdicts.
Its images are quicker and cooler than the anima's: the wind, the horse, the hero-lover who arrives from elsewhere.

great-mother.name: Great Mother
great-mother.oneLine: Giver and devourer: earth, womb, cave and the realm of the Mothers.
body: The Great Mother holds both sides of origin: the nourishing earth and the swallowing dark. She is goddess, cave, well and tree before she is anyone's personal mother.
Her images sit at the instinct end of the spectrum: dense, warm and terrestrial.

child.name: Child
child.oneLine: Beginning and futurity: the newborn possibility of wholeness.
body: The Child is the archetype of what has not yet happened: the threatened newborn, the abandoned and invincible one, the little figure who turns out to hold the whole.
It is dawn-coloured in this atlas: soft, rising, unfinished.

kore.name: Kore
kore.oneLine: The maiden: youth before transformation, soul in bloom and in descent.
body: Kore is the maiden figure who is carried off, hidden or crowned: Persephone in spring and in Hades. She stands between the anima and the Self, both a young girl and an intimation of wholeness.
Her images are green and early, always about to change.

trickster.name: Trickster
trickster.oneLine: Shape-shifter and fool: archaic, unconscious cunning that unsettles the order.
body: The Trickster is the joker and boundary-crosser: half divine, half beast, careless of rules and strangely generative. Out of his blunders something new, and sometimes something healing, gets made.
Mercurius, the quicksilver spirit of alchemy, carries the trickster into the laboratory.

hero.name: Hero
hero.oneLine: The struggle toward light: slayer of the dragon, bearer of renewed life.

definitionPick.starts: Taken purely as a psychologem the hero

body: The Hero is consciousness fighting its way out of the mother, the monster and the night. Solar and lucid, the hero's journey is descent and return; its dangers are inflation and identification with the light.
Its colour is the lucid white-gold of the risen sun.

wise-old-man.name: Wise Old Man
wise-old-man.oneLine: Spirit as meaning: the guide who appears when thought has run out.

definitionPick.starts: Mostly, therefore, it is the figure of a 'wise old man'

body: The Wise Old Man is meaning given a face: a sage, a magician, a prophet, sometimes an animal or a gnome. He comes with knowledge the dreamer lacks, and with the reflection and resolve to use it.
He sits near the spirit end of the spectrum: fine, clear, cool.

mana-personality.name: Mana-Personality
mana-personality.oneLine: The charged, fascinating figure who holds numinous power over the ego.

definitionPick.starts: The hero is the protagonist of God's transformation

body: The mana-personality is the figure who has absorbed more power than any person should carry: magician, prophet, hierophant. The ego is fascinated by such a figure and tempted to become it.
It sits between the wise old man and the hero, closer to the numinous than either.

psychopomp.name: Psychopomp
psychopomp.oneLine: Guide of souls across thresholds: mediator between conscious and unconscious.
body: The Psychopomp leads across: Hermes with the dead, the bird that carries the soul out of the vessel, the unexpected companion on the road. It is a function more than a face, and it keeps the passage between worlds open.
Its colour is dusk, between the instinct and spirit ends.

syzygy.name: Syzygy
syzygy.oneLine: The divine pair: masculine and feminine joined as one image of wholeness.
body: The Syzygy is the paired opposite: king and queen, sun and moon, anima and animus held in one picture. In alchemy it is the conjunction at the centre of the work; in dreams it often arrives as a wedding.
Its images show up wherever a tradition has pictured the two as one.

one.name: One
one.oneLine: The One: Monoïmos's single Monad, which Jung reads as the nature of the self.

definitionPick.starts: This Man is a single Monad

body: In Aion (CW9ii ¶340–341, 1951) Jung gives Hippolytus's report of the single Monad of Monoïmos and says that this paradoxical idea describes the psychological nature of the self as conceived by a thinker of the second century.
In his letter 63 to Pauli (October 1953) Jung writes that 1 is the One, absolute, nondivisible, and thus the unconscious, the beginning.

two.name: Two
two.oneLine: The dyad: the division of the One, the pair; and the conjoined two of the mandala.

definitionPick.starts: Psychologically the self is a union

body: In letter 63 to Pauli (October 1953) Jung lists 2 as the division of the One, the pair, the connection, the difference. In Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶805–806, 1958) he writes that since a state of confusion is generally the result of a psychic conflict, the dyad, the conjoined two, is also associated with the mandala in practice, and that the complexio oppositorum of Cusanus coincides with the dyad among the symbols of the self.
In Aion (CW9ii ¶426, 1951) he writes that psychologically the self is a union of conscious (masculine) and unconscious (feminine).

three.name: Three
three.oneLine: The triad: the Trinity's number, usually a masculine number, a relative totality.
body: Jung writes that dogma insists three are one while denying that four are one, and that since olden times uneven numbers have been regarded as masculine and even numbers as feminine (CW12 ¶25, Psychology and Alchemy, 1944). In Aion (CW9ii ¶351, 1951) he writes that three can be regarded as a relative totality and, where it refers to the self, should be understood as a defective quaternity or a stepping-stone towards it.

In the Trinity essay (CW11 ¶246) he writes that three is not a natural coefficient of order but an artificial one, and, in letter 63 to Pauli (October 1953), where the scan is damaged at the start of the line, that 3 is the son, the first masculine number.

four.name: Four
four.oneLine: The quaternity: the minimum of a whole judgment; the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys.
body: Jung writes that the quaternity forms the logical basis for any whole judgment and that the natural minimal division of the circle is a quaternity (CW11 ¶246). In Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶805, 1958) he writes that the structure of the mandala is arithmetical, because whole numbers are likewise archetypes of order, and that this is true particularly of the number 4, the Pythagorean tetraktys.
In Aion (CW9ii ¶381, 1951) he calls the quaternity an organizing schema par excellence.

five.name: Five
five.oneLine: The quinta essentia: the circle divided into four with the centre, the quincunx.

definitionPick.starts: In the centre is the egg encircled

body: In Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶737–738, 1958) the ground structure of a painting by Birkhäuser is a quincunx, which Jung calls a symbol of the quinta essentia, identical with the Philosophers' Stone: the circle divided into four with the centre, or the four functions of consciousness with their unitary substrate, the self. He writes that in his work with patients the quaternity symbol crops up very frequently and the pentad very rarely (CW10 ¶775).
The caption of a mandala by a woman patient, with an egg encircled by the snake at its centre, calls it exceptional in having a pentadic structure (CW9i, pdf p382).

six.name: Six
six.oneLine: The hexad: a totality symbol in Jung, and the number of creation and generation.

definitionPick.starts: The self is by definition the centre

body: Jung writes that the hexad is a totality symbol, four as the natural division of the circle and two as the vertical axis (CW10 ¶771, 1958), and that according to old tradition the number 6 means creation and evolution, being a coniunctio of 2 and 3 (CW9i ¶679).
Von Franz writes in Number and Time that six is the first numeral of the series to represent the sum of its divisors, one, two and three.

seven.name: Seven
seven.oneLine: The seven planetary gods, who took up their abode in the seven metals of alchemy.
body: Jung writes that the seven refer to the gods of the planets, or the seven metals (CW14 ¶563), and that the antique company of seven gods later took up their abode in the seven metals of alchemy (CW12 ¶468). Of the Book of Enoch he writes that the seven stars were originally the seven great Babylonian gods and had by the time of Enoch's revelation become the seven Archons (CW12 ¶298). The stages of the alchemical work are marked by seven colours associated with the planets (CW14 ¶390).

Jung writes no essay on seven; the passages show where he names it. Pauli, in a letter of 1936, says of the seven in his own early dreams that it is an indication of the birth of the anima; that is Pauli's reading, and the page gives it in his name.

eight.name: Eight
eight.oneLine: The ogdoad: a double quaternity, a totality at once heavenly and earthly.
body: In Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶692–693, 1958) Jung writes that eight is a double quaternity and, as an individuation symbol in mandalas, plays almost as great a role as the quaternity itself, and that the ogdoad is a totality symbol. In Mysterium Coniunctionis (CW14 ¶8) he writes that the double quaternio or ogdoad stands for a totality, for something that is at once heavenly and earthly, spiritual or corporeal.

Of the series of seven and eight he writes that the seven form an uninterrupted series while the step to the eighth involves hesitation or uncertainty, as with three and four in the Axiom of Maria (CW14 ¶574), and that this may be a reason why the eighth is feminine, the mother of a new series (CW14 ¶579).

nine.name: Nine
nine.oneLine: Nine: in Dorn, the One as the novenary foetus; the Ennead; a line that changes.
body: In his account of Gerhard Dorn in Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon (CW13, 1942), Jung writes that the One is the midpoint of the circle, the centre of the triad, and also the novenary foetus, that is, as the number nine to the ogdoad or as the quintessence to the quaternity; the note to the sentence cites Dorn's Duellum animi cum corpore.

Elsewhere Jung writes that a company of gods described as nine often proves to be ten or more (CW12 ¶84); that a line of six or nine in the I Ching has an inner tension so great that it changes into its opposite (CW11 ¶996); and, in a note, that Jezoth, that is Yesod, is the ninth and middle Sefira in the lowest triad (CW14 ¶634).

ten.name: Ten
ten.oneLine: Ten: unity perfectly unfolded in Jung; the whole multiplicity of existence in von Franz.
body: In his interpretation of a dream of the numbers eight and eleven (CW10 ¶692, 1958) Jung gives, from the traditional symbolism, ten as the perfect unfolding of unity and the numbers one to ten as the significance of a completed cycle, so that 10 + 1 = 11 denotes the beginning of a new cycle.

Jung names the tetraktys for the number four (CW10 ¶805); von Franz writes that the Pythagorean tetractys is the sum of 1, 2, 3 and 4, which is 10. In Number and Time she also reports Fa-tsang's simile of ten copper coins, in which ten signifies the whole inexhaustible multiplicity of existence.

court-knight.name: The Knight
court-knight.oneLine: Court of the Thoth deck: Yod of the Name, the Father; the fiery part of each element.
body: In Crowley's Name the Knight stands for Yod, the first letter of the Tetragrammaton, which he says symbolises the Father who is Wisdom. In the pagan series the Knight is the Father, called Knight because he rides a horse. In each element the Knight is the most active part of its energy.

The tie to the Wise Old Man is a reading made here. Crowley gives the Father as Wisdom, but the Knight's qualities in his text are activity, fierceness and pride, which an amplification would also set beside the hero.

court-queen.name: The Queen
court-queen.oneLine: Court of the Thoth deck: Hé of the Name, the Mother; the watery part of each element.
body: The Queen stands for the letter Hé of the Name. Crowley says that letter is traditionally consecrated to the Great Mother. In the pagan series she is the Mother, and in each suit she is the watery part of the element: its power of reception and reflection.

The tie to the Great Mother is a reading made here, drawn from the letter Hé and from Crowley's own words on the Mother. The Queens' qualities in his text, adaptability and calm authority, are kept beside it.

court-prince.name: The Prince
court-prince.oneLine: Court of the Thoth deck: Vau of the Name, the Son; the airy part of each element.
body: The Prince is the letter Vau of the Name, the Son of the pagan series. In each element he is the airy part, swift and strong in the Wands, subtle in the Cups and purely intellectual in the Swords. Crowley refers the Son to the number six, the centre of his system.

The tie to the child is a reading made here. Crowley writes that the child Horus is born of the union of the two parents, and that the Aeon of Horus is the Aeon of the Child; the reading takes the Son to the child on that basis, not on his own equation.

court-princess.name: The Princess
court-princess.oneLine: Court of the Thoth deck: Hé final of the Name, the Daughter; earthy part of each element.
body: The Princess is the letter Hé final of the Name, the Daughter of the pagan series. Crowley says she represents the ultimate issue of the original energy, its crystallisation and materialisation. He calls her the perfect Maiden, and in the legends the forsaken Widow after the Prince's death. She has no zodiacal attribution in his text, only a quadrant of the heavens.
The tie to the kore is a reading made here, drawn from the perfect Maiden and from the Daughter that Crowley places on the earth of Malkuth.
